title: Neuro-Symbolic AI: Why the Next Real Step Isn't a Bigger Model
excerpt: A practical guide to neural interpretation, explicit constraints and checked decisions: build a small validator, understand specification gaps, and design an evaluation that separates prediction from execution.
content:
An assistant can produce a convincing explanation for a decision it was never allowed to make. That is the practical problem that interests me about neuro-symbolic AI: how do we combine a model's ability to interpret messy inputs with a system that can check whether a proposed action is actually valid?

This is a technical tutorial and a reading of selected research, not a report of a new model or benchmark I trained. The examples below are deliberately small so that the boundary between prediction and verification stays visible.

## Start with a problem that has an exact answer

Imagine a warehouse assistant reading a request: “Send four units of the blue adapter to our Dhaka office.” Natural language understanding helps identify the product, quantity and destination. It cannot establish that the warehouse has four units, that the requester can ship stock, or that the destination is permitted.

Those facts come from inventory and access-control systems. A fluent explanation does not replace them. If a model invents an item identifier and the backend accepts it, the failure is at the interface between interpretation and execution, even if the response sounds sensible.

The useful decomposition is: interpret the request, construct a candidate operation, validate the candidate against current facts, then execute only the validated operation. Each stage should leave a record that can be inspected independently.

## What neural and symbolic components contribute

A neural component is useful when the input has many surface forms: misspellings, incomplete descriptions, paraphrases or visual ambiguity. It proposes a representation. In the warehouse example, it might map “blue adapter” to a shortlist of catalogue entries rather than guessing one definitive identifier.

A symbolic component manipulates explicit objects and constraints. A rule can require a positive integer quantity, a permitted destination, a specific capability and sufficient unreserved stock. The same input and facts should produce the same validation result. This makes the decision easier to reproduce than an explanation sampled from a language model.

Neither component is automatically reliable. An explicit rule can be wrong, outdated or incomplete. A perfectly implemented validator can approve an incorrectly interpreted request. Hybrid design moves uncertainty into named boundaries; it does not make uncertainty disappear.

## Two research examples that clarify the idea

The 2024 [AlphaGeometry paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06747-5) combines a neural language model that proposes useful geometric constructions with a symbolic deduction engine. Its reported result of 25 solved problems from a 30-problem olympiad geometry set belongs to that particular system and evaluation. It is not evidence that a generic chatbot can reliably prove arbitrary statements.

[DeepProbLog](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.10872) offers a different kind of integration: neural predicates participate in a probabilistic logic program. It is useful to compare these examples because “neuro-symbolic” names a family of designs, not one architecture. Generating candidates for a solver, learning predicates inside a logic program and validating an agent's tool call are related ideas with different guarantees.

My engineering interpretation is to ask which component proposes an answer, which checks it, and exactly what the check establishes. That question is more informative than attaching the hybrid label to a diagram.

## Design the interface before the prompt

For the warehouse example, a candidate should contain an operation type, a catalogue identifier, a quantity and a destination identifier. It should not contain an executable SQL statement or a free-form instruction for the inventory service.

Separate the user's words from authoritative facts. The candidate may say `quantity=4`; the inventory service supplies `available=3`. The model must not provide both values and then “verify” its own arithmetic. Likewise, capability checks must use the authenticated caller rather than a role string extracted from the message.

Keep a reference to the original request and the version of the policy used. If a rejection is questioned later, you need to distinguish “the request was parsed incorrectly” from “the applicable rule rejected it.” Without that separation, prompt changes become an unreliable substitute for debugging.

## A small executable validator

This Python example illustrates the checking boundary. It is not the implementation of AlphaGeometry or a complete inventory service.

```python
def validate_pick(candidate, *, available, capabilities, destinations):
    errors = []
    quantity = candidate.get("quantity")
    if candidate.get("operation") != "pick":
        errors.append("unsupported operation")
    if type(quantity) is not int or quantity <= 0:
        errors.append("quantity must be a positive integer")
    if "stock:pick" not in capabilities:
        errors.append("missing capability")
    if candidate.get("destination") not in destinations:
        errors.append("destination is not permitted")
    if type(quantity) is int and quantity > available:
        errors.append("insufficient stock")
    return errors

request = {"operation": "pick", "quantity": 4, "destination": "dhaka"}
assert validate_pick(request, available=3,
    capabilities={"stock:pick"}, destinations={"dhaka"}) == [
        "insufficient stock"
    ]
assert "quantity must be a positive integer" in validate_pick(
    {**request, "quantity": True}, available=10,
    capabilities={"stock:pick"}, destinations={"dhaka"})
```

The second assertion is intentional: in Python, booleans are integer subclasses. A loose integer check can accept `True` as a quantity. Details like this show why schema validation deserves tests rather than a sentence in a system prompt.

Passing validation still does not reserve inventory. Another request could consume the stock between the check and the write. Execution must recheck the relevant invariant inside the storage system's concurrency boundary. Logical validation and transactional correctness solve different problems.

## A checked result has a limited scope

Suppose the validator approves the request. What has been established? Only that the supplied candidate meets the implemented rules under the supplied facts. It has not established that the blue adapter was interpreted correctly, that the stock count is physically accurate, or that the policy is appropriate.

This is the specification gap. A system can be correct with respect to a formal description while that description fails to represent the real requirement. The [Lean documentation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Elaboration-and-Compilation/) makes the distinction between elaboration and kernel checking concrete: checking a formal term is a separate task from deciding what statement should have been formalized.

For a product, I would expose this distinction in the interface. “Checked against stock and destination policy” is more precise than “verified answer.” If interpretation remains ambiguous, ask the user to choose the product instead of presenting a certificate for the wrong one.

## Decide whether you need a solver

Ordinary predicates are often enough for a small set of rules. A solver becomes useful when several choices interact: which orders can be fulfilled from several warehouses, with capacity limits and mutually exclusive assignments?

In a constraint formulation, the model proposes relevant entities or a problem description; the solver searches for an assignment satisfying the encoded constraints. The [Z3 guide](https://microsoft.github.io/z3guide/docs/logic/intro/) is a starting point for understanding satisfiability checking. Solver output still needs careful interpretation: a result depends on the formula, supported theory and resource limits. An unknown or timed-out result should not quietly become approval.

Do not add a solver to hide unclear product requirements. First write down what constitutes a valid action, which inputs are trusted and what should happen when a fact is missing. A short explicit validator can reveal those requirements faster than a large reasoning framework.

## Evaluate the pipeline by failure type

One overall accuracy number conceals too much. I would construct separate test groups for interpretation, schema validation, rule enforcement and execution. Give the interpreter ambiguous catalogue descriptions. Give the validator invalid quantities and unavailable destinations. Give the executor concurrent requests for the final item in stock.

For model experiments, compare a direct-answer baseline, structured output alone, structured output with validation, and validation with bounded repair. Keep the underlying tasks and resource budgets comparable. Measure task success alongside invalid-action acceptance, unnecessary rejection, latency and clarification frequency. These are proposed evaluation dimensions, not results measured for this tutorial.

Test the repair loop too. A rejected candidate should receive specific, minimal feedback. Unlimited retries can increase cost, encourage guessing and make an apparently successful system depend on repeated attempts. Stop after a defined budget and preserve the rejection reason.

## Preserve evidence through the final explanation

The final model response should be generated from the executed result, not from the original optimistic plan. If the service reserved three units, the explanation must not claim four were shipped. A validated tool call and an ungrounded final sentence are still an inconsistent product.

I would return a typed result containing the action identifier, actual state transition and any unresolved conditions. The explanation layer may translate that result into readable language, but it should not invent additional actions. This makes the narrative downstream of the evidence.

## A practical exercise

Extend the validator with a per-request quantity limit. Then construct an input that satisfies the schema but violates the new rule. Next, simulate two requests competing for the same stock. Finally, deliberately supply an incorrect product identifier and observe that all the arithmetic checks can pass.

Those three failures live at different boundaries. Understanding which boundary failed is the main lesson I want a reader to take away. Reliable reasoning systems need clear specifications, authoritative facts and inspectable decisions as much as they need better predictions.

## Sources and further reading

- [Trinh et al., AlphaGeometry, Nature (2024)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06747-5): a neural proposal mechanism paired with symbolic geometry deduction.
- [Manhaeve et al., DeepProbLog (2018)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.10872): neural predicates in probabilistic logic programming.
- [Lean language reference: elaboration and compilation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Elaboration-and-Compilation/): the boundary between constructing and checking formal terms.
- [Microsoft Z3 guide](https://microsoft.github.io/z3guide/docs/logic/intro/): satisfiability and explicit constraints.

The warehouse example, validator and suggested experiments are original teaching examples in this article. They are not benchmark results from the cited papers.
imageAlt: Neural representations combine with explicit rules to support hybrid reasoning and checked outputs.
imageCaption: A conceptual view of neuro-symbolic reasoning. The illustration summarizes the relationship between learned representations and explicit rules; it is not an architecture or experimental result from a specific paper.

title: The Reversal Curse: Your LLM Knows "A is B" but Not "B is A"
excerpt: Understand directional factual recall, distinguish parameter learning from in-context reasoning, build paired probes, and evaluate bidirectional retrieval without overstating the original research.
content:
Suppose a model learns that a fictional researcher, Mira Sen, created a fictional dataset called Lantern-47. You ask who created Lantern-47 and it cannot retrieve Mira Sen. The information appears simple, but the question approaches it from the opposite direction.

The reversal curse is a useful way to study the gap between encountering a fact and being able to retrieve it under a different query. This article explains the distinction, outlines an experiment a reader can build, and connects it to retrieval and evaluation design. It does not report a fine-tuning experiment I personally ran.

## What the original result actually says

In [Berglund et al.'s reversal-curse study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.12288), models fine-tuned on synthetic name-description facts often answered queries following the training order but failed to generalize to the reverse order. The authors also reported an asymmetry for celebrity-parent questions in the GPT-4 version they evaluated: 79% in one direction and 33% in the other. These are historical results from that evaluation, not performance figures for today's models.

The paper distinguishes facts learned through parameter updates from facts supplied in the current context. Its finding does not mean that a model given a relationship directly in a prompt is universally unable to reverse it. Missing that distinction turns a specific research result into an exaggerated claim about reasoning.

## Directional prediction is not a reversible lookup table

An autoregressive training objective rewards predictions of the next token given earlier tokens. If a sequence places a name before a description, the training signal directly concerns predicting that continuation. It does not explicitly create a database index from every description back to its name.

In probability terms, `P(description | name)` and `P(name | description)` are different conditional distributions. Bayes' rule relates them only when the appropriate marginal probabilities and model assumptions are available. A text generator is not automatically executing that calculation when asked a question.

Shared parameters can still produce generalization, and training data may contain both orders. Therefore the objective alone is not a proof that reverse retrieval must always fail. It explains why reversibility is not guaranteed. The difference matters: an architectural intuition is not a substitute for measuring a particular model and dataset.

## Distinguish identity from an asymmetric relation

“A is B” is convenient shorthand, but natural-language relationships have types. “Mira created Lantern-47” reverses into “Lantern-47 was created by Mira,” not “Lantern-47 created Mira.” A parent relationship is not symmetric, and a person can have several children.

Before testing reversal, define the inverse query precisely. If several answers are valid, a scorer that accepts only one name will undercount correct responses. If the description is not unique, failure to produce the intended entity may be an ambiguity problem rather than a reversal failure.

For an experiment, I would use unique invented entity-description pairs with explicit relation labels. For a product, I would store the relation as structured data and generate inverse queries according to the relation type. Treating all sentence reversals as logical identity produces a misleading benchmark.

## Build an experiment that controls contamination

Use synthetic names and descriptions that are not facts a pretrained model is likely to know. Generate separate groups of forward-only facts, reverse-only facts and facts shown in both directions. Reserve additional entity pairs for controls and keep the evaluation prompts out of the training set.

Record the base checkpoint, tokenizer, fine-tuning configuration, training seed, number of exposures per fact and decoding settings. Without these, a change in answer rate can be caused by a training-budget difference rather than the intervention you intended to test.

Do not treat a prompt-only test as a reproduction of parameter learning. Prompting with the complete fact and then asking the inverse question measures contextual use. Fine-tuning changes model parameters. Both experiments are useful, but they answer different questions and should be reported separately.

## Construct paired probes before running the model

The following code creates a small evaluation fixture. It does not train a model or produce an accuracy claim.

```python
facts = [
    {"entity": "Mira Sen", "artifact": "Lantern-47"},
    {"entity": "Oren Vale", "artifact": "Cobalt-19"},
]

def paired_probes(fact):
    return {
        "forward": {
            "prompt": f"Which dataset did {fact['entity']} create?",
            "answer": fact["artifact"],
        },
        "reverse": {
            "prompt": f"Who created the dataset {fact['artifact']}?",
            "answer": fact["entity"],
        },
    }

def normalize(text):
    return " ".join(text.casefold().strip().rstrip(".").split())

probes = [paired_probes(fact) for fact in facts]
assert normalize(" Mira  Sen. ") == normalize("Mira Sen")
assert probes[0]["reverse"]["answer"] == "Mira Sen"
```

A small normalizer prevents whitespace and final punctuation from becoming false failures. It is not a complete semantic scorer. An answer such as “It was created by Mira Sen” needs a clearly specified extraction rule or a separate grading procedure. Do not change that procedure after seeing which model wins.

## Look beyond two aggregate percentages

For each fact, record whether the forward and reverse answers are correct. This produces four groups: both correct, forward only, reverse only and neither. The forward-only group is especially useful because it separates an order-sensitive retrieval failure from cases where the model learned neither direction.

I would also report reverse accuracy conditioned on forward success. Keep the unconditional score alongside it: a model with very few forward successes can look deceptively good on a small conditional subset. Include sample sizes and uncertainty intervals rather than treating a few examples as a stable measurement.

Use several prompt templates and multiple seeds. A model may recognize one phrasing but fail another. Keep paraphrase robustness separate from reversal robustness so that improving one does not conceal deterioration in the other. Inspect representative errors manually; incorrect names, abstentions and extra unsupported claims are different failure modes.

## Separate memory retrieval from contextual reasoning

Run the same reverse question under three conditions: no supporting fact in the prompt, the correct fact in the prompt, and an unrelated distractor in the prompt. If supplying the fact changes the answer, that is evidence that context availability matters. It does not by itself identify how the fact is represented in the weights.

A fourth condition can supply a conflicting fact. Then you are testing how the system resolves evidence and prior associations, which is a separate design question. Label it accordingly. Combining all four conditions into one “reasoning score” makes the result harder to interpret.

This distinction is valuable when debugging an application. If an answer becomes correct when a document is retrieved, spending more effort on retrieval may be more productive than adding a longer chain-of-thought instruction. First identify what evidence the model actually receives.

## Mitigation one: represent both query directions

If you control a training dataset, explicitly include legitimate inverse queries for the same facts. This should not be confused with assuming that examples about unrelated facts will automatically teach universal inversion. Keep the relation type and possible multiple answers intact.

[Golovneva et al.'s reverse-training work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13799) studies training with forward and transformed reverse strings, preserving selected substrings such as entities. That procedure is more specific than “reverse every character.” It is a training intervention with its own compute and data accounting, not a one-line prompting trick.

For an application experiment, compare alternatives under explicit budgets. Doubling training material while leaving the baseline unchanged creates a different comparison from matching the number of tokens or the compute used. Describe which question you are answering before reporting improvement.

## Mitigation two: make retrieval bidirectional

A structured store can retain `creator=Mira Sen` and `artifact=Lantern-47` as fields in one record. Both query directions can then retrieve the same evidence. The generator is responsible for wording an answer from that record rather than reconstructing the relationship entirely from its parameters.

A vector index is not automatically a bidirectional knowledge graph. An inverse question may still retrieve the wrong passage. Test retrieval recall for both query forms, inspect the retrieved context, and preserve provenance at the record level. If retrieval fails, a fluent answer with a citation-shaped decoration does not fix the problem.

For operational systems, I prefer being able to inspect the record and query path. That does not make all retrieval systems superior to fine-tuning; it makes this particular failure easier to locate and correct.

## What this result should not make us claim

It does not establish that models store every fact in only one direction, that reverse reasoning is impossible, or that every hallucination is a reversal error. It also does not justify projecting the behavior of a tested historical checkpoint onto a newer one without evaluation.

The useful conclusion is narrower and more actionable: exposure to a relationship is insufficient evidence that your system can retrieve it under every required query. Test the actual query directions your users depend on.

## An exercise for a retrieval application

Create twenty fictional project-maintainer records. Ask both “Who maintains this project?” and “Which project does this person maintain?” Evaluate retrieval separately from answer generation. Add a person who maintains two projects and a project with two maintainers.

That small change forces you to confront relation cardinality, scoring and ambiguity. The exercise teaches more than collecting a screenshot of one failed celebrity question. You end with a test fixture that can survive changes to the embedding model, prompt or generator.

## Sources and further reading

- [Berglund et al., The Reversal Curse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.12288): the original synthetic-fact experiments and their contextual-learning distinction.
- [Official experiment repository](https://github.com/lukasberglund/reversal_curse): implementation and reproduction material from the authors.
- [Golovneva et al., Reverse Training to Nurse the Reversal Curse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13799): a specific reverse-training intervention.

The fictional dataset, fixture code and proposed product evaluation above are teaching material, not measurements from those studies or results from my own fine-tuning run.
imageAlt: A learned forward relationship from A to B contrasts with an incomplete reverse relationship from B to A.
imageCaption: The reversal curse, illustrated: learning a directional fact does not automatically establish the inverse. AI-generated conceptual illustration.

title: Building Complete Legal Aid for Production
excerpt: An engineering walkthrough of authorization, state transitions, reconnect recovery, document access and bounded AI drafting, with concrete failure scenarios and an honest evaluation plan.
content:
A legal-aid platform is a coordination system before it is an AI interface. Citizens, lawyers and administrators see different information, messages arrive after the browser disconnects, documents have an access history, and a drafting request may remain unfinished when an external model times out. A polished dashboard can conceal those problems during a demo without solving them.

Complete Legal Aid is the project behind this walkthrough. My portfolio describes my work as full-stack development and AI integration. Here I focus on the engineering boundaries a reader can reuse: authorization, state transitions, event delivery, document access and model-assisted drafting. Examples are simplified design patterns, not instructions for a particular legal matter or claims of an independently audited system.

## Begin with actors and operations

“Citizen dashboard,” “lawyer dashboard” and “admin dashboard” are navigation concepts. They are not access-control rules. A useful authorization model names the caller, operation and resource: can this citizen view this case attachment, can this lawyer edit this draft, can this administrator approve this specific transition?

A role alone is too broad. Two citizens share a role but must not automatically see each other's documents. A lawyer's relationship to a case can change, so assignment is a fact to check at the time of access rather than a permission permanently implied by their profession.

Start with a matrix of operations and relationships. For each operation, define the allowed role, required resource membership, relevant case state and the response when access is denied. That matrix becomes a source for endpoint checks and negative tests. It also exposes product questions that a frontend alone cannot answer.

## Trace one workflow across the boundaries

Consider a citizen submitting documents, a lawyer reviewing them and an AI service proposing a draft. The upload endpoint authorizes the citizen against the case. The storage layer assigns an internal object identifier. A review event becomes visible to the assigned lawyer. A drafting request reads only the authorized material, produces a draft and records its status.

No single step should infer that every later step is permitted. A successful upload does not grant every connected WebSocket client access. A drafting tool should not receive a storage URL simply because a browser previously displayed it. Each boundary needs an explicit contract.

For debugging, attach a correlation identifier to the workflow and stable identifiers to its case, document and drafting attempt. Do not use the raw document body as a debugging shortcut. A trace should explain where an operation failed without becoming a second uncontrolled copy of sensitive content.

## Authenticate the connection and authorize the object

The inspected realtime code includes per-user streams and a case-presence consumer. The presence connection checks authentication, account status and case access before joining the case's group. That is the right kind of boundary to look for: group membership is a consequence of authorization, not a substitute for it.

The [Django Channels security guide](https://channels.readthedocs.io/en/stable/topics/security.html) also explains why WebSocket origin checks matter. An authenticated browser session does not make every origin safe. Connection authentication, allowed origins and resource-level authorization address different risks and should not be collapsed into one “secured socket” checkbox.

Long-lived connections need a policy for changed permissions. If a lawyer is reassigned after connecting, what happens to existing subscriptions? Recheck authorization for protected operations and decide how revocation reaches active connections. A check performed once at connection time does not establish permanent entitlement.

## Model transitions instead of loosely related booleans

An appointment can be requested, accepted, cancelled or completed. A draft can be queued, running, ready or failed. Several independent booleans can accidentally encode impossible combinations, such as a draft being both ready and failed.

Define permitted transitions and make them explicit at the service boundary. Include the expected current state in an update so two callers cannot silently overwrite one another's decisions. If two operations race, one should detect the conflict and return a useful response rather than invent a new state through timing.

This teaching example demonstrates a transition check without prescribing the project's database schema:

```python
ALLOWED = {
    "queued": {"running", "cancelled"},
    "running": {"ready", "failed"},
    "ready": set(),
    "failed": {"queued"},
    "cancelled": set(),
}

def transition(current, target):
    if target not in ALLOWED.get(current, set()):
        raise ValueError(f"invalid transition: {current} -> {target}")
    return target

assert transition("running", "ready") == "ready"
```

The function checks a local rule. A production update also needs a transaction or conditional write to ensure that `current` has not changed since it was read. A pure Python state machine cannot by itself coordinate concurrent workers.

## A successful write and a delivered event are different facts

Suppose a database transaction saves a message, then the process crashes before publishing the notification. The message exists, but another browser sees no realtime update. Reversing the order can produce a notification for data that later rolls back.

An outbox design addresses this by saving a durable event record with the business write and delivering it separately. The worker can retry delivery; consumers must tolerate duplicates. This is a proposed reliability pattern, not a claim that every Complete Legal Aid event currently uses an outbox.

[Django's transaction documentation](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/topics/db/transactions/) describes atomic blocks and commit hooks. A commit hook is useful for avoiding publication before commit, but it is not itself a durable queue. The distinction becomes visible when the process dies after commit and before the hook finishes its external work.

## Design reconnect as recovery rather than a fresh start

Realtime delivery should improve responsiveness, not be the only route to truth. After reconnecting, a client needs a way to retrieve authoritative state and identify events it may have missed. Stable message identifiers and a cursor make that recovery possible.

The interface should distinguish queued, acknowledged and failed sends. If a user retries the same message after a timeout, an idempotency key can prevent duplicate creation. The server decides whether the operation already completed; the browser should not infer failure merely because its acknowledgement was lost.

Test this deliberately: disconnect immediately after sending, reconnect, then retry. The desired outcome is a single durable message with a recoverable status. Count what the server stored, not only what appeared during an uninterrupted browser session.

## Treat document access as a separate operation

An opaque filename is not an access-control system. The service that resolves a document identifier should verify the caller's relationship to the case. If using time-limited download links, define their lifetime and the consequences of forwarding a link to someone else.

Uploads require size limits, permitted formats and careful handling of filenames and content. A browser-provided MIME type is a hint rather than proof. Keep access logs focused on identifiers and outcomes. Avoid logging the body of an uploaded document simply because a request failed.

Deletion and revocation need their own behavior. A document removed from a dashboard should not remain indefinitely available through an old public path. An engineering review should inspect the storage route and authorization path, not only the UI's visibility condition.

## Bound the authority of an AI drafting workflow

A drafting service should receive the smallest authorized context needed for its task. Give it a narrow output contract and a set of approved operations. Treat document contents as source material, including when a document contains text that looks like an instruction to the assistant.

The inspected agent guardrail module includes jurisdiction framing, a non-advice disclaimer and regular-expression redaction for obvious identifiers in logs. These are useful controls, but regex matching is incomplete and a disclaimer does not establish factual correctness or enforce tool authorization. Server-side access checks must stand independently of model compliance.

Keep the output labeled as a draft and preserve the distinction between source text, model-generated text and reviewed text. If a referenced passage cannot be located in the source material, do not turn that absence into a confident citation. Evidence traceability is part of the workflow, not a decoration added after generation.

## Measure drafting quality beyond time saved

A short generation time can coexist with a long review time. I would separate queue delay, model latency, time to a reviewable draft and time spent correcting unsupported or missing content. Report the task definition and sample size before claiming an efficiency improvement.

The earlier blog included a 45-minute-to-under-3-minute comparison without the benchmark protocol needed to interpret it. This article does not present that comparison as a validated general result. A useful future evaluation would use a consistent set of drafting tasks, a documented review rubric and a clear separation between automated output and human acceptance.

For the application itself, useful tests include another citizen's document identifier, a revoked lawyer assignment, a repeated callback, an unavailable model provider and a worker restart during generation. Those tests examine boundaries that an ordinary happy-path demo misses.

## Deployment is part of the application contract

The frontend, HTTP API, socket service, background workers and storage depend on different runtime conditions. Check health separately and expose readiness only when a service can perform its essential function. A process listening on a port is not evidence that its queue or database is usable.

Keep production secrets outside the browser bundle, terminate TLS correctly and document backups and restore procedures. Rollback needs to account for schema compatibility as well as container versions. A new image that expects a new column cannot necessarily be replaced by an old image without a plan.

These are deployment requirements to verify, not a blanket certification of the project. The [Django deployment checklist](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/howto/deployment/checklist/) is a useful primary reference for framework-level checks.

## A concrete exercise for the reader

Implement a draft job with four states and an idempotency key. Simulate a crash after saving the result but before sending the browser its notification. Restart the worker, reconnect the client and verify that the result appears once.

Then repeat the retrieval using an account that has no case relationship. The same data should remain recoverable for the authorized user and unavailable to the unauthorized one. Reliability and access control must both survive the recovery path.

## Sources and project context

- [Complete Legal Aid project case study](/projects/complete-legal-aid): portfolio context and project scope. The implementation repository is private; access can be requested through the project page.
- [Django Channels: security](https://channels.readthedocs.io/en/stable/topics/security.html).
- [Django: database transactions](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/topics/db/transactions/).
- [Django: deployment checklist](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/howto/deployment/checklist/).

The state-machine code, failure scenarios and outbox discussion are explanatory designs. They should not be read as claims that every proposed reliability improvement is already implemented or independently audited.
imageAlt: Citizen, lawyer and administrator workflows connect messaging, documents, bookings, payments and AI-assisted drafting.
imageCaption: Conceptual overview of the workflows discussed in this case study. This AI-generated illustration is not a screenshot or a security audit.

title: ChefMate: NLP + ML Pipeline from User Input to Recipe
excerpt: Follow ingredient normalization and cosine retrieval, uncover a filtered-index mismatch in the current code, and work through a corrected candidate-search example and practical evaluation plan.
content:
ChefMate starts with a practical question: what can someone cook with the ingredients they already have? That sounds like a recommendation problem, but much of the difficult work happens before ranking. Ingredient names arrive as plurals, regional names, multiword phrases and typing mistakes. A model cannot retrieve the right recipe consistently if the query and the recipe database disagree about what the same ingredient is called.

This walkthrough is based on the project's source inspected on October 20, 2026. It distinguishes the current implementation from improvements proposed below. In particular, the current training file uses `CountVectorizer` with cosine nearest-neighbour retrieval; describing that snapshot as a TF-IDF implementation would be inaccurate.

## Define the retrieval contract

A useful response is more than a recipe name. It should show which requested ingredients matched, which ingredients are missing and what any displayed score means. A person choosing dinner can then decide whether buying two missing ingredients is acceptable.

The query can be represented as a set of canonical ingredient identifiers plus explicit filters for cuisine, diet and meal type. The output should retain stable recipe identifiers. Ranking may use vectors internally, but the user-facing explanation should come from identifiable ingredients rather than a mysterious similarity value.

I would keep “recipe coverage” separate from “query overlap.” If a user has tomato, onion, egg and rice, a recipe requiring tomato, onion and salt has two of three required ingredients available. Its coverage is about two thirds. That is different from the fraction of the user's four ingredients used by the recipe, and neither number is a probability that the dish will be good.

## Normalize without erasing meaning

ChefMate's normalization helper lowercases text, uses spaCy lemmas, applies a curated synonym map and optionally performs fuzzy correction against known vocabulary. The source uses RapidFuzz, rather than the FuzzyWuzzy library named in an earlier description.

[spaCy's lemmatizer documentation](https://spacy.io/api/lemmatizer) explains the role of lemmas and pipeline dependencies. In an ingredient search system, lemmatization is only one stage: it does not tell you that aubergine and eggplant are regional names for the same ingredient, or that coconut milk should remain distinct from ordinary milk.

Normalization needs a policy, not just a string-cleaning function. Preserve meaningful phrases, retain a mapping to the original text and make the same canonicalization rules apply during indexing and querying. If the database encodes `green_onion` while a synonym path returns `green onion`, splitting on whitespace changes one ingredient into two tokens. That is a representation inconsistency, not an issue a larger nearest-neighbour model will solve.

## Fuzzy similarity is a candidate signal

The current helper accepts the best vocabulary match at a threshold of 80 on its similarity scale. That number is a rule in the source, not a measured accuracy percentage. [RapidFuzz's documentation](https://rapidfuzz.github.io/RapidFuzz/Usage/fuzz.html) describes several scorers with different behavior; an arbitrary threshold does not have the same interpretation across all of them.

A short string deserves special caution. Two ingredient names can differ by only a few characters while referring to different foods. I would show uncertain corrections for confirmation, reject an empty vocabulary safely and compare the best match with the second-best match. A narrow gap is evidence of ambiguity even when the top score exceeds a threshold.

Keep fixtures for spelling errors that should be corrected and near-matches that must remain distinct. The cost of a wrong substitution can exceed the cost of returning fewer recipes. This article does not treat fuzzy text matching as an allergy or food-safety guarantee.

## Understand the baseline before changing it

`CountVectorizer` creates a vocabulary and counts token occurrences. With cosine distance, nearest-neighbour search compares the direction of count vectors. The current training script fits that representation and a brute-force `NearestNeighbors` model, then persists the model, vectorizer and dataframe together.

[Scikit-learn's feature-extraction guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/feature_extraction.html#text-feature-extraction) distinguishes count-based features from TF-IDF weighting. TF-IDF can reduce the relative influence of terms common across many recipes, but that is a candidate experiment, not an automatic upgrade. Common ingredients may still matter to a user's ability to cook the dish.

Start with a transparent baseline such as ingredient-set overlap. Compare a binary count representation, ordinary counts and TF-IDF under the same test queries. Otherwise, a more complicated model may appear useful simply because it was compared against an undocumented or broken baseline.

## A filtering bug that changes the meaning of an index

The inspected prediction code filters the recipe dataframe, resets its index and transforms those filtered rows into `X`. It then calls `kneighbors` on the previously fitted model, which was trained over the full dataset, and uses returned neighbour positions to select rows from the filtered dataframe. The computed filtered `X` is not used to fit that search.

Those positions refer to different collections. Imagine training rows `[A, B, C, D]` and a filter retaining `[B, D]`. A returned position `1` from the original model identifies B. Position `1` in the filtered dataframe identifies D. The code can therefore attach a distance to the wrong recipe, or discard a valid neighbour because its original position exceeds the filtered length.

This is a code-review finding, not a published fix to ChefMate. It illustrates a general rule: an index has meaning only relative to the collection that created it. Resetting dataframe indices does not remap an already fitted neighbour model.

## Keep candidate rows and retrieval indices aligned

One correction strategy is to fit a candidate search over the filtered matrix. Another is to retrieve from the full index and apply filters using stable recipe identifiers, accepting that a fixed retrieval depth may miss eligible results. For a small dataset, the first option is easier to reason about.

Here is a standalone teaching example using an intentionally tiny corpus. It is not copied from the production application:

```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

recipes = [
    {"id": "r1", "diet": "vegetarian", "items": "tomato onion rice"},
    {"id": "r2", "diet": "other", "items": "chicken onion rice"},
    {"id": "r3", "diet": "vegetarian", "items": "egg tomato onion"},
]
vectorizer = CountVectorizer(binary=True)
matrix = vectorizer.fit_transform([row["items"] for row in recipes])
candidate_positions = [i for i, row in enumerate(recipes)
                       if row["diet"] == "vegetarian"]
candidate_matrix = matrix[candidate_positions]
search = NearestNeighbors(metric="cosine", algorithm="brute")
search.fit(candidate_matrix)
query = vectorizer.transform(["tomato onion"])
distances, local_positions = search.kneighbors(query, n_neighbors=2)
ranked_ids = [recipes[candidate_positions[i]]["id"]
              for i in local_positions[0]]
assert set(ranked_ids) == {"r1", "r3"}
```

In a real endpoint, check for an empty candidate set and an all-zero query vector before searching. Limit the neighbour count to the number of candidates. Those cases should return an understandable response rather than a library exception or an arbitrary ranking.

## Make ranking and explanation agree

ChefMate exposes matched and missing ingredient lists and sorts results using an overlap score. That is a valuable explanation surface, but the definition should be consistent. Use sets of canonical ingredients for both numerator and denominator. Counting duplicate tokens in one part of the computation while deduplicating another can distort the score.

Separate retrieval from re-ranking explicitly. Cosine similarity can shortlist plausible recipes; a second stage can prioritize coverage, missing-item count or user preference. Keep those stages visible in debugging output. If a user sees a lower-coverage recipe above a higher-coverage one, you should be able to explain which ranking rule caused the order.

Avoid calling an overlap score “confidence.” It is a computed property of two sets, not a calibrated probability. A recipe can share most ingredients yet require a missing item essential to the dish.

## Evaluate with query families and useful labels

Create a small judged query set before tuning thresholds. Include clean input, plurals, regional synonyms, misspellings, multiword ingredients, unseen terms, restrictive filters and empty input. Keep separate labels for canonicalization correctness and recipe relevance.

For ranking, Precision@k measures how many returned items are judged relevant. Recall@k asks how many relevant items were recovered from the judged candidate universe. If relevance is graded, a ranking measure such as NDCG can reflect that a nearly cookable recipe is more useful than a weak match. Specify the relevance rubric; metrics without a labeling policy are difficult to interpret.

Prevent duplicate recipes from appearing in both tuning and evaluation sets. Record baseline results, then change one stage at a time. The earlier “70% improvement” claim had no accompanying benchmark in the material inspected, so I do not carry it forward as a measured result.

## Persist the representation as one versioned unit

The persisted vectorizer, dataset and search model must describe the same vocabulary and row order. Add a schema version, dataset hash, dependency versions and normalization version to the artifact metadata. A model file that loads successfully can still be semantically incompatible with a new dataframe.

[Scikit-learn's persistence documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/model_persistence.html) discusses compatibility and the risk of pickle-based loading. Treat model artifacts as trusted deployment inputs; do not deserialize files submitted by arbitrary users. Load the approved artifact once per worker rather than reopening a large file on every request, and measure memory use before adding more workers.

## What I would improve next

I would fix index alignment first, then unify canonical ingredient identifiers and add normalization fixtures. Only after those changes would I compare count features with TF-IDF or embeddings. A stronger representation cannot compensate for selecting the wrong dataframe row.

The most reusable lesson is that retrieval quality depends on contracts between stages: canonicalization, candidate selection, vectorization, neighbour lookup and explanation. Testing those contracts makes a modest model easier to trust and a future model easier to evaluate.

## Sources and implementation references

- [ChefMate repository](https://github.com/Tanjamul-Azad/ChefMate), especially `utils.py`, `train_model.py` and `predict.py`: the implementation snapshot discussed above.
- [spaCy lemmatizer reference](https://spacy.io/api/lemmatizer).
- [RapidFuzz scorer reference](https://rapidfuzz.github.io/RapidFuzz/Usage/fuzz.html).
- [Scikit-learn feature extraction](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/feature_extraction.html#text-feature-extraction), [nearest neighbours](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/neighbors.html) and [persistence](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/model_persistence.html).

The small corpus and correction example are explanatory material. The proposed evaluation has not been presented here as a completed benchmark.

title: Care Companion: Designing an AI + IoT Healthcare Rover
excerpt: Learn how to separate sensing, vision, control and delivery; handle stale data and placeholder measurements; and design bounded buffers, meaningful benchmarks and failure-injection tests.
content:
A rover that displays a camera feed, sensor readings and a caregiver dashboard looks like one system. In practice, those functions operate on different clocks. A camera produces frames, a sensor can fail halfway through a read, a network request can block, and a motor command must stop being valid when its source becomes stale.

Care Companion is my project context for exploring those boundaries. This article is an engineering walkthrough of a prototype, not a clinical validation report. It separates features described in the project from source-level observations and proposed reliability improvements. The goal is to teach how to reason about a small embedded system when components are slow, disconnected or wrong.

## Start with the age of information

“Real-time” is not a single property. A display can refresh quickly while showing old data. A detector can process many frames per second while its input queue grows, leaving a controller to react to where someone was several seconds ago.

For each signal, record when it was sampled, when it was received and when it was acted upon. The difference between sampling and action is often more useful than an isolated throughput number. Include the unit, source and a quality indicator so that a plausible numeric value is not mistaken for a trustworthy measurement.

I would define freshness requirements separately for motor commands, camera detections, environmental readings and dashboard history. A historical chart can tolerate delayed delivery. A command that moves hardware should not remain active indefinitely because a network packet was never followed by a stop message.

## Distinguish prototype hardware paths

The portfolio describes a Raspberry Pi and Arduino rover arrangement. The inspected repository also contains a Pi-side reader using GPIO and I2C devices directly, together with a Django dashboard, Channels and Celery components. These are not interchangeable wiring descriptions. A deployment needs to name the specific board, sensor, interface and software path actually in use.

That distinction matters when writing documentation. A diagram that combines every component ever tried can imply an integrated configuration that was never tested. I would version the hardware configuration alongside the software and identify which adapters are enabled for a particular prototype.

For the architecture discussion below, the separation is logical: acquisition collects readings, vision produces detections, control decides permitted motion, and the application persists and displays observations. Those boundaries can run on separate boards or processes without changing the questions each stage must answer.

## Do not let network delivery own the sampling clock

A loop that reads a sensor and immediately posts the result over HTTP inherits the network request's delay. When the server is slow, the sampling rate changes. If the request has no timeout, the acquisition loop may stop making progress entirely.

Separate acquisition from delivery through a bounded buffer. The producer samples and timestamps; the sender batches or transmits with explicit timeouts and retry limits. Decide what to do when the buffer fills. Dropping an old routine reading can be acceptable for a live display, while an alert may need durable delivery.

For a serial-based adapter, [pySerial's API](https://pyserial.readthedocs.io/en/latest/pyserial_api.html) documents read and write timeout behavior. Configure those limits and frame the messages deliberately. “Read until a newline eventually arrives” is not a recovery strategy for a disconnected or partially transmitting device.

## A reading needs provenance and quality

A useful reading envelope includes a device identifier, a sequence number, the measurement name, a unit, timestamps and a quality state. Use explicit states such as valid, unavailable, stale and simulated. Do not substitute zero for a failed read: zero is a value that a graph may plot and an alert rule may evaluate.

Device clocks can drift or reset. Keep a server-received timestamp in addition to the device's sampling timestamp, and use a monotonic clock for elapsed-time checks within a process. A timestamp without a defined clock source creates false precision.

Sequence numbers also need a restart strategy. Pair them with a boot or session identifier so that a device returning to sequence zero after reboot does not look like an endless stream of duplicate old readings. This is a small protocol detail with a large effect on recovery.

## A source-level limitation worth making visible

The inspected Pi sensor reader includes a pulse calculation explicitly marked as a placeholder. It maps an ADC value into a displayed BPM range rather than deriving heart rate from detected pulse intervals. Its gas conversion also scales a raw ADC value without establishing a sensor-specific calibrated concentration measurement.

Those observations are important because a number with a familiar unit can look authoritative on a dashboard. A placeholder conversion should remain labeled simulated or uncalibrated; it should not silently become evidence of physiological accuracy. The article does not provide clinical thresholds or treat this prototype as a substitute for validated monitoring equipment.

A useful improvement is to persist the quality flag with the value and propagate it through the API and chart. The UI should not be the only place that knows a reading was simulated, because later exports and alert jobs also consume the data.

## Keep frame latency bounded

Computer vision creates another producer-consumer problem. If capture runs faster than inference, an unbounded queue accumulates old frames. The detector may remain busy while the control system receives increasingly stale observations.

For a live tracking display, a latest-frame buffer can be preferable to preserving every frame. The following example demonstrates that policy with a thread-safe queue; it is not the deployed rover implementation:

```python
from queue import Queue, Empty, Full

frames = Queue(maxsize=1)

def offer_latest(frame):
    try:
        frames.put_nowait(frame)
        return
    except Full:
        pass
    try:
        frames.get_nowait()
    except Empty:
        pass
    try:
        frames.put_nowait(frame)
    except Full:
        pass  # Another producer won; memory still remains bounded.

offer_latest({"sequence": 1})
offer_latest({"sequence": 2})
assert frames.get_nowait()["sequence"] == 2
```

This buffer sacrifices completeness to preserve freshness. It is inappropriate for a task that must retain every frame for offline analysis. The [Python queue documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/queue.html) provides the blocking and non-blocking semantics; the application still chooses its data-loss policy.

## Benchmark the entire vision path

Capture, resizing, preprocessing, inference, postprocessing, rendering and transmission all contribute to observed delay. Measure them separately, then measure end-to-end age at the point where a detection is used. Include warm-up behavior, image resolution, model variant, thread count and processor temperature.

The [MobileNets paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.04861) describes efficient convolutional building blocks, while the [SSD paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.02325) describes a single-stage detection approach. Neither establishes the frame rate of an unspecified model on this project's Raspberry Pi configuration.

The old blog stated approximately 60 FPS without a reproducible benchmark configuration in the material inspected. I have removed that as a measured project result. A more useful report would give sustained throughput, latency percentiles, dropped-frame counts and behavior while sensing and network delivery run concurrently.

## Control must reject stale commands

A motor controller should receive a constrained command rather than an unrestricted stream of prose or raw model output. Define allowed directions, limits and a short validity period. A watchdog can stop accepting a command when the controller has not received a fresh authorized update.

Avoid equating a person detection with permission to move. Perception provides an observation with uncertainty; a control policy decides whether movement is permitted. Missing detections, multiple people, occlusion and an outdated frame should all have defined behavior.

For a prototype review, I would ask whether the stop path remains available during inference overload and network loss. A software check in a busy browser is not equivalent to a local control mechanism. The required hardware safeguards depend on the physical setup and must be evaluated as part of that setup.

## Alerts and reminders need different delivery semantics

A reminder is a scheduled occurrence, not a side effect of a browser being open. The repository's Celery-based application structure provides a place for background jobs, but adding a queue alone does not guarantee timely or duplicate-free delivery.

Assign each scheduled occurrence a stable identifier. A retried task should find whether that occurrence already completed before repeating an external action. [Celery's task documentation](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/userguide/tasks.html) discusses idempotence, acknowledgements and I/O timeouts; the exact retry and acknowledgement settings still need to match the operation.

Separate “condition observed,” “notification sent,” “notification received” and “someone acknowledged it.” They represent different events. A server returning HTTP 200 for an alert request does not establish that a caregiver saw it or took action.

## Design the dashboard around uncertainty

Show the last update time and quality status alongside the value. Render stale or unavailable data explicitly rather than freezing a green indicator at its last valid state. On reconnect, fetch authoritative recent state instead of assuming that the live stream delivered every observation.

Keep historical storage and live display separate enough to recover after a socket interruption. Protect patient-related data through authenticated APIs and resource-level authorization. Screenshots and demo modes should use synthetic records rather than accidentally exposing real personal information.

The visual design question is therefore not only “does the chart look smooth?” It is “can someone distinguish a current observation from an old, missing or simulated one?” Honest uncertainty is part of the interface contract.

## A failure-injection exercise

Run the acquisition and delivery components with synthetic input. Delay the server response, disconnect the network, restart the device and inject an invalid reading. Record whether memory stays bounded, whether sequence identities remain interpretable and whether the dashboard marks stale data.

Then slow the vision worker and verify that the latest-frame policy actually limits observation age. Repeat with a burst of alerts and check that routine telemetry cannot indefinitely delay them. These are proposed tests, not completed reliability measurements for the prototype.

The system becomes easier to improve once each failure has a visible owner: acquisition quality, buffering policy, control validity, delivery recovery or presentation. That is the central lesson of an AI-and-IoT project for me. Integration is the behavior of the boundaries, especially when one side stops cooperating.

## Sources and project context

- [Care Companion repository](https://github.com/Tanjamul-Azad/Care-companion), including the dashboard README and `raspi/sensor_reader.py` inspected for this article.
- [Python queue reference](https://docs.python.org/3/library/queue.html) and [pySerial API](https://pyserial.readthedocs.io/en/latest/pyserial_api.html).
- [Celery task guide](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/userguide/tasks.html).
- [MobileNets](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.04861) and [SSD](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.02325): background on efficient vision and single-stage detection.

The code example and failure exercises are teaching material. Hardware-specific performance, calibrated sensing accuracy and clinical suitability require their own evidence.
imageAlt: A conceptual rover connects vision, processing, sensing and control with a caregiver dashboard.
imageCaption: Conceptual illustration of an AI and IoT rover system. The hardware layout and dashboard are illustrative, not photographs or exact specifications of our prototype.
